prompt: According to the law of diminishing marginal utility, what happens as a consumer eats more slices of pizza in one sitting?

options.text: Total satisfaction falls with the very first slice
Each extra slice adds less satisfaction than the last
The market price of pizza rises with each slice
Consumers switch to complementary goods immediately

explanation: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit; as consumption rises in the short run, each additional unit adds less value.

trap_notes.a: Total satisfaction still rises at first; only the added gain per slice shrinks.
trap_notes.c: One buyer's hunger does not automatically raise the restaurant's menu price.
trap_notes.d: Diminishing marginal utility describes satisfaction per unit, not switching goods.
trap_notes.default: Each additional unit consumed in one sitting brings smaller added satisfaction.

prompt: Why do economists classify childhood vaccinations as creating a positive externality?

options.text: Private clinics earn profits without any regulation
Vaccinated people pay higher taxes on medical care
Third parties gain lower disease risk without paying
Insurance firms eliminate all deductibles for patients

explanation: A positive externality occurs when a transaction creates spillover benefits for bystanders who were not part of the purchase.

trap_notes.a: Provider profit is a private return, not a spillover benefit to third parties.
trap_notes.b: Taxes are government transfers, not an external health benefit.
trap_notes.d: Insurance billing rules do not define an economic externality.
trap_notes.default: Positive externalities deliver unpriced benefits to people outside the transaction.

prompt: When a chemical plant dumps untreated waste into a river, why does an unregulated market overproduce that chemical?

options.text: The plant ignores external cleanup costs borne by others
Downstream residents pay the plant to increase output
Government subsidies force the plant to run at capacity
Consumers value polluted water more than clean water

explanation: Because the firm pays only private production costs and not social pollution costs, it produces past the socially optimal level.

trap_notes.b: Downstream residents suffer harm; they do not pay the plant to pollute.
trap_notes.c: Overproduction happens even without subsidies when pollution is free.
trap_notes.d: Clean water has value, but its loss is left out of the firm's private ledger.
trap_notes.default: Unpriced external costs lead firms to produce more than society prefers.

prompt: Which pair of traits defines a pure public good such as national defense or a lighthouse beam?

options.text: High retail price and private ownership
Scarce supply and strict user fees
Elastic demand and rapid depreciation
Non-rivalrous use and non-excludable access

explanation: A pure public good is non-rivalrous (one person's use leaves no less for others) and non-excludable (non-payers cannot be blocked).

trap_notes.a: Private ownership and high prices describe private goods, not public goods.
trap_notes.b: User fees exclude non-payers, which violates non-excludability.
trap_notes.c: Elasticity and depreciation apply to many private goods as well.
trap_notes.default: Pure public goods are both non-rivalrous and non-excludable.

prompt: What economic problem explains why open-access ocean fisheries often suffer rapid overfishing?

options.text: Fishers face high property taxes on ocean waters
Individual fishers gain the catch while all share depletion
Seafood demand stays constant regardless of price
Central banks restrict loans for new fishing boats

explanation: In the tragedy of the commons, a shared, rivalrous resource is overused because each user captures private gains while costs spread.

trap_notes.a: Open-ocean fisheries lack private ownership and property taxes.
trap_notes.c: Demand elasticity does not cause open-access depletion by itself.
trap_notes.d: Tight boat loans would reduce fishing effort rather than increase it.
trap_notes.default: Shared rivalrous resources are overused when private gains exceed private costs.

prompt: Which feature distinguishes monopolistic competition, such as neighborhood restaurants, from perfect competition?

options.text: Only one firm legally operates in the entire city
Firms face insurmountable barriers to market entry
Many firms sell differentiated products via branding
Government regulators set identical menu prices

explanation: Monopolistic competition has many sellers and easy entry like perfect competition, but each firm differentiates its product.

trap_notes.a: A single legal seller describes a monopoly, not monopolistic competition.
trap_notes.b: High entry barriers characterize monopolies and oligopolies.
trap_notes.d: Firms set their own prices based on product differentiation.
trap_notes.default: Product differentiation among many sellers defines monopolistic competition.

prompt: Why are municipal water pipes and local electric grids considered natural monopolies?

options.text: One network supplies the market at lower cost than rivals
Consumers prefer buying utilities from foreign firms
Water and electricity require zero fixed infrastructure
Small startups can duplicate power lines cheaply

explanation: High fixed infrastructure costs create strong economies of scale, making a single regulated provider cheaper than duplicate networks.

trap_notes.b: Local utilities are tied to physical grids, not foreign consumer preferences.
trap_notes.c: Utilities require massive upfront fixed investments in pipes and lines.
trap_notes.d: Duplicating power lines is prohibitively expensive and wasteful.
trap_notes.default: Economies of scale make one grid cheaper per customer than competing grids.

prompt: Why is the supply of most manufactured goods more price elastic in the long run than in the short run?

options.text: Consumers forget about price changes after one year
Short-run factories face zero resource constraints
Governments ban price adjustments during the short run
Firms can build new plants and adjust capacity over time

explanation: Over a longer horizon, producers can expand factories, train workers, and enter or exit markets in response to price shifts.

trap_notes.a: Supply elasticity depends on producer flexibility, not consumer memory.
trap_notes.b: Short-run production is constrained by fixed plant size and equipment.
trap_notes.c: Supply elasticity reflects physical production limits, not price bans.
trap_notes.default: Long-run time lets firms expand capacity and adjust all inputs.

prompt: In the circular flow model of an economy, what role do households play in factor markets?

options.text: They sell labor and capital to firms in exchange for income
They purchase finished consumer goods from retail stores
They print currency and set overnight interest rates
They collect corporate taxes from manufacturing plants

explanation: Households supply labor, land, and capital in factor markets and earn wages, rent, and profits in return.

trap_notes.b: Buying finished goods takes place in product markets, not factor markets.
trap_notes.c: Printing currency and setting policy rates are central bank functions.
trap_notes.d: Collecting taxes is a government fiscal role, not a household factor role.
trap_notes.default: Households are sellers of productive inputs in factor markets.

prompt: What does a higher Gini coefficient, closer to 1.0 than to 0.0, indicate about a country's income distribution?

options.text: Faster annual growth in real industrial output
Greater inequality in how income is shared
Lower inflation across consumer price indexes
Higher average wages for entry-level workers

explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person holds all income), measuring income inequality.

trap_notes.a: GDP growth measures output expansion, not income distribution.
trap_notes.c: CPI tracks price inflation, not how income is divided.
trap_notes.d: A high Gini score reflects wider gaps, not higher entry-level pay.
trap_notes.default: Values closer to 1.0 on the Gini index signal higher income inequality.

prompt: Why do economists classify a flat state sales tax on groceries as a regressive tax?

options.text: High-income shoppers pay a higher tax rate at checkout
Stores remit the tax only during economic recessions
Low-income families spend a larger share of income on food
Federal courts prohibit states from taxing retail sales

explanation: Because lower-income households spend a greater percentage of their income on necessities, a flat sales tax takes a larger share.

trap_notes.a: All shoppers face the same flat rate at the register regardless of income.
trap_notes.b: Sales taxes apply year-round, not just during downturns.
trap_notes.d: Most U.S. states legally collect retail sales taxes.
trap_notes.default: A tax is regressive when it takes a larger percentage of lower incomes.

prompt: In the short-run Phillips curve, what inverse relationship did economists historically observe?

options.text: Higher tariffs paired with lower domestic prices
Higher savings rates paired with zero investment
Lower interest rates paired with higher unemployment
Lower unemployment paired with higher wage inflation

explanation: The short-run Phillips curve illustrates a tradeoff in which tighter labor markets (lower unemployment) push wages and prices up.

trap_notes.a: Tariffs raise import prices rather than lowering domestic prices.
trap_notes.b: Higher savings generally support investment rather than eliminating it.
trap_notes.c: Lower interest rates usually stimulate hiring and reduce unemployment.
trap_notes.default: The short-run Phillips curve links low unemployment with rising inflation.

prompt: In a fractional-reserve banking system, how do commercial banks expand the broader money supply?

options.text: They lend out excess reserves beyond required cash
They mint gold coins inside local branch vaults
They lock every customer deposit inside a safe
They collect federal income taxes on payroll checks

explanation: When banks keep only a fraction of deposits in reserve and lend the rest, those loans become new deposits across the system.

trap_notes.b: Commercial banks do not mint coins; central banks issue base currency.
trap_notes.c: Holding 100 percent of deposits in vaults prevents credit creation.
trap_notes.d: Tax collection is a government treasury function, not bank lending.
trap_notes.default: Lending excess reserves creates new checking deposits and expands money.

prompt: Which example best illustrates investment in human capital to raise long-run economic productivity?

options.text: Buying shares of a foreign technology company
Training workers in advanced robotics and coding
Storing cash inside a commercial bank savings account
Importing crude oil for winter home heating

explanation: Human capital consists of the education, skills, and health that make workers more productive.

trap_notes.a: Buying stock is financial investment, not an upgrade to worker skills.
trap_notes.c: Holding cash in savings does not directly expand worker productivity.
trap_notes.d: Importing heating oil is resource consumption, not human capital.
trap_notes.default: Education and job training build human capital and raise productivity.

prompt: If a savings account pays a 5 percent nominal interest rate while annual inflation is 3 percent, what is the real interest rate?

options.text: 8 percent purchasing-power gain
5 percent purchasing-power gain
2 percent purchasing-power gain
15 percent purchasing-power gain

explanation: The real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus inflation (5% - 3% = 2%), showing actual purchasing-power growth.

trap_notes.a: Adding inflation to the nominal rate overstates real returns; inflation erodes value.
trap_notes.b: Five percent is the nominal rate before adjusting for rising prices.
trap_notes.d: Real interest is found by subtracting inflation, not multiplying rates.
trap_notes.default: Subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal rate gives the real interest rate.
